definition.text: A North American land planning and engineering approach, called LID, that manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure.

facts.text: It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime by infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source.
Similar terms include SuDS in the UK and water-sensitive urban design in Australia.
It began in Prince George's County, Maryland in 1990, because conventional detention ponds were not cost-effective and missed water quality goals.
Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize hydrological impact, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution.
Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and rainwater harvesting.
Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks.
It can remove the need for stormwater ponds on expensive land, letting developers build more homes on the same plot.
In some municipalities it is a cost-effective way to reduce combined sewer overflows.

definition.text: A nature-based urban planning model from China that uses green infrastructure, not just drains, to manage urban water and floods.

facts.text: The name reflects how green landscapes store, slow and soak up surface water like a sponge.
Its philosophy is to retain water at the source, slow its flow, clean it naturally and adapt where it collects, the reverse of grey infrastructure's pipes, reservoirs and walls.
Hard urban surfaces can raise surface flow from 10% to 60% and cut infiltration to nearly zero.
Proposed by landscape architect Kongjian Yu, it became national Chinese policy in 2014 after the 2012 Beijing flood killed 79 people.
Pilots began in 16 districts in 2015, growing to 87 cities by 2017.
Guidelines aim for cities to collect and use 70 percent of rainwater, on 20 percent of urban area by 2020 and 80 percent by 2030.
Studies show it reduces runoff and improves water quality, but monitoring data are scarce and 19 of 30 pilot cities have flooded since.

definition.text: Demolishing a dam to return natural water flow to a river.

facts.text: The case for removal weighs dams' benefits, such as hydropower, flood control, irrigation and navigation, against their harms.
Dams can reduce primary productivity, biodiversity and native species, and ageing brings weakness, sediment build-up and high maintenance costs.
About 900 US dams were removed between 1990 and 2015, and by 2015 the rate was 50 to 60 a year.
Many removals aim to restore river habitat and native fish, as in the Elwha Ecosystem Restoration.
Releasing trapped sediment can rebuild habitat downstream, but toxic sediment can do harm, as when PCBs were released after a Hudson River dam was removed.
Removal is always costly, and the cost is usually shared between the owner and government.
The European Commission counts at least 150 000 barriers in European rivers that no longer serve a purpose.
The EU Biodiversity Strategy aims to restore free flow to 25,000 kilometres of river by 2030.

definition.text: The four common ways of removing a dam, chosen mainly by how the sediment behind it is handled.

facts.text: Notch and release drains the reservoir slowly through cut notches so the ecosystem can adjust; it can take over a year.
Rapid release is quickest and cheapest but can cause severe flooding and erosion downstream.
Dig and dewater, usually the most expensive, removes dried sediment for safe disposal, needed when it contains toxins.
Retained sediment leaves the sediment in place and reroutes the river around the site.

title: Alternatives to dam removal

definition.text: Ways of reducing a dam's harm without removing it, such as better equipment, environmental flows and fish ladders.

facts.text: Fewer than 1% of US dams are being considered for removal.
Varying the water released by season mimics natural flow changes.
The effectiveness of fish ladders is debated, though some fish pass rather than none.
Plans for decommissioning and river restoration should be drawn up well before a dam reaches its design life.

contested_note: Sources debate how effective fish ladders are at letting fish reach spawning grounds.
